title: The Tempest
author: William Shakespeare
setting: A ship in a storm, then an unnamed island, across a single afternoon
lengthNote: Around 2,000 lines — one of the shortest plays in the Folio
summary: A magician who was once Duke of Milan raises a storm to bring his enemies ashore on the island where he has lived in exile for twelve years. He has the whole afternoon planned before the play begins, and the interest lies in watching a man with absolute power discover what he actually wants to do with it. Almost alone among Shakespeare's plays it keeps to a single place and a few hours, so that the action and the performance take roughly the same time.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Tempest
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering; modern editions differ by a line or two. Ariel's songs are printed inside another speaker's text in some settings, and are attributed here to Ariel.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After reports of the 1609 Sea Venture wreck reached London, and before the recorded court performance of November 1611.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto exists. The First Folio prints it first in the volume, at the head of the comedies.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: Shipwreck pamphlets, Florio's Montaigne, Ovid and the court masque, combined rather than adapted.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act I Scene 2 alone runs to about a third of the play.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A storm, and the twelve years behind it
structure.summary: The shipwreck is staged first and explained second. Prospero then tells Miranda the history she has never been told, wakes and dispatches Ariel, insults Caliban, and steers Ferdinand into meeting his daughter — four interviews in one scene, each conducted by a man who already knows how it ends.

scenes.title: The ship
scenes.summary: Courtiers get in the way of the crew; the Boatswain tells them rank means nothing to the weather.

scenes.title: The island
scenes.summary: Prospero recounts the usurpation to Miranda, sets Ariel back to work, curses Caliban and arranges Ferdinand's arrival.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Two conspiracies, one serious and one drunk
structure.summary: On one part of the island Gonzalo imagines a commonwealth with no trade, law or labour and is mocked for it; within fifty lines Antonio has talked Sebastian into murdering his brother. On another, Caliban meets a butler with a bottle and decides that a new master is the same thing as freedom.

scenes.title: The courtiers
scenes.summary: Gonzalo's utopia is laughed down; Antonio persuades Sebastian to kill the sleeping Alonso, and Ariel wakes them.

scenes.title: The bottle
scenes.summary: Trinculo shelters under Caliban's cloak, Stephano arrives with wine, and Caliban swears allegiance to a drunkard.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A betrothal, a plot and a banquet that vanishes
structure.summary: Miranda proposes marriage to Ferdinand while her father watches unseen. Caliban lays out a workable murder — take the books first — and is repeatedly interrupted by Ariel's mimicry. The act ends with the courtiers accused of their old crime by a spirit dressed as a harpy.

scenes.title: The log-pile
scenes.summary: Ferdinand carries wood; Miranda offers herself as wife, and Prospero approves from a distance.

scenes.title: The conspiracy
scenes.summary: Caliban explains how to kill Prospero; Ariel sows confusion by throwing his voice.

scenes.title: The harpy
scenes.summary: A banquet appears and disappears; Ariel indicts Alonso, Antonio and Sebastian to their faces.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A masque, broken off
structure.summary: Prospero gives the young couple a wedding entertainment performed by spirits, and then stops it mid-dance because he has remembered Caliban. The interruption is the hinge of the play: the most beautiful thing he makes is abandoned because of the one creature he cannot govern by art.

scenes.title: The masque and the line of clothes
scenes.summary: Iris, Ceres and Juno bless the betrothal; Prospero breaks off the show, then traps the conspirators with a rack of glittering clothes.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Forgiveness, and the end of the magic
structure.summary: Ariel describes the suffering of the charmed courtiers and Prospero chooses mercy — before he has heard a word of apology from any of them. He abjures his art, restores Ferdinand to his father, claims Caliban as his own, frees Ariel, and steps forward to ask the audience for release.

scenes.title: The circle, and the epilogue
scenes.summary: Prospero breaks his staff, forgives his brother, discovers the lovers at chess, frees Ariel and asks for applause as absolution.

characters.name: Prospero
characters.role: The exiled Duke of Milan, and the island's magician
characters.summary: He lost a dukedom by preferring his library to government and has spent twelve years acquiring a power no government could match. Almost every event in the play is something he has arranged, which makes the one decision he has not rehearsed — to forgive rather than punish — the only genuine action in it.
characters.clue: A scholar who lost a dukedom to his own reading, and who runs an island the way a director runs a rehearsal room, down to the storm.

characters.name: Miranda
characters.summary: She has met three people in her life and remembers none of her own history until her father decides she should. Her instincts are consistently better than his: she pities the shipwrecked before she knows who they are, and she proposes marriage herself rather than waiting to be arranged into it.
characters.clue: She has seen three human faces in her life, weeps for strangers drowning, and asks a log-carrier to marry her before he can ask her.

characters.name: Ariel
characters.role: A spirit of the air, bound to Prospero's service
characters.summary: Everything the audience calls Prospero's magic is in fact Ariel's labour: the storm, the songs, the harpy, the masque, the invisible mischief. The relationship runs on a promise of freedom that is repeatedly deferred, and the play's most surprising moment is Ariel telling a human what pity would look like.
characters.clue: Invisible, tireless and unpaid: the one who actually raises the storm, sings the drowned father's song and asks, again, when the promise will be kept.

characters.name: Caliban
characters.role: Son of the witch Sycorax; the island's earlier inhabitant
characters.summary: He welcomed Prospero, showed him the fresh water and the fertile ground, and was enslaved for it after attempting to rape Miranda. The play gives him the case against his master and the best verse about the island, and then refuses to let either cancel the other out.
characters.clue: He showed the newcomer where the fresh springs were and has been carrying his firewood ever since; he speaks the loveliest lines about the island he says is his.

characters.name: Ferdinand
characters.summary: He is separated from the ship, told his father has drowned, and set to carrying logs — a trial that has no purpose except to make Miranda seem hard-won. He accepts the labour without complaint, which is the only test Prospero can devise and the only one he passes.

characters.name: Alonso
characters.summary: He put Antonio into Prospero's dukedom and spends the play believing he has lost his son as a consequence. Grief, not argument, is what breaks him: by Act V he is the only one of the three guilty men who says anything resembling an apology.

characters.name: Antonio
characters.role: Prospero's brother, the usurping Duke of Milan
characters.summary: He took a dukedom once and, within an hour of washing ashore, is arranging a second murder for someone else's benefit. He is forgiven in the last scene and does not reply, a silence that most productions have to make a decision about.
characters.clue: He took his brother's title while the man was reading, and washes ashore only to start talking another younger brother into the same crime.

characters.name: Sebastian
characters.summary: A mocker of other men's speeches who turns out to need only one conversation to be talked into killing his sleeping brother. He is the proof that Antonio's crime was not a single aberration but a piece of ordinary political reasoning.

characters.name: Gonzalo
characters.summary: He is the reason Prospero survived: he stocked the leaking boat with food, water and the books. His imagined commonwealth without money or magistrates is mocked on stage as nonsense, and it is also the only vision in the play of an island run by nobody.

characters.name: Stephano
characters.role: Alonso's butler, washed ashore with a butt of wine
characters.summary: Given a bottle and a worshipper, he declares himself king of the island within a scene. His plot against Prospero is the same plot as Antonio's, played by a drunk, and the parallel is the play's sharpest joke about how little ambition requires.

themes.name: Rule and service
themes.summary: Every relationship on the island is a version of master and servant: Prospero and Ariel, Prospero and Caliban, Prospero and Ferdinand at the log-pile, Stephano and his new subject. The play sets them side by side so that the differences between labour, slavery, apprenticeship and worship become visible.
themes.development: The first act establishes three servants with three grievances; the last frees one, claims another and says nothing at all about the third.

themes.name: Whose island is it
themes.summary: Caliban's claim is stated plainly in the first act and never refuted, only overruled. Shakespeare gives the dispossessed party the historical facts and the finest description of the place, and gives the occupier the power, which is why the play has been unignorable in the century of decolonisation.
themes.development: 'This island's mine' in 1.2 sets the terms; Gonzalo's commonwealth in 2.1 imagines an island belonging to nobody; the play ends without saying who is left on it.

themes.name: Magic as theatre
themes.summary: Prospero's art is indistinguishable from stagecraft: costumes, music, entrances, illusions, an interrupted masque. When he describes his own show dissolving he uses the words 'the great globe itself', spoken in a theatre of that name, and the metaphor stops being a metaphor.
themes.development: The storm is staged in 1.1, exposed as a production in 1.2, perfected in the masque of 4.1, renounced in 5.1, and handed to the audience in the epilogue.

themes.name: Freedom and what is mistaken for it
themes.summary: Three characters want to be free and each means something different by it: Ariel wants release from service, Caliban wants his island back, and Stephano's crew want a bottle and a crown. The play is careful to make the drunkards' freedom song ridiculous without making Caliban's demand ridiculous.
themes.development: Ariel asks in 1.2 and is refused; Caliban sings of a new master in 2.2; Ariel is released in the last twenty lines, and Prospero then asks to be freed himself.

themes.name: Revenge given up
themes.summary: Prospero has the power to do anything he likes to the men who ruined him, and the decisive scene is the one in which he decides not to. What makes it strange is the timing: he chooses mercy after a spirit has described their suffering to him, and before any of them has asked for it.
themes.development: Twelve years of grievance are recited in 1.2; the harpy indicts the guilty in 3.3; 5.1 turns on Ariel's remark that he would feel pity if he were human.

themes.name: Nature and nurture
themes.summary: Prospero insists that Caliban is a devil on whom nurture will never stick, having spent years teaching him. Miranda, raised on the same island by the same man with the same books, is his counter-example, and the play leaves the argument standing unresolved between them.
themes.development: Caliban is taught language in 1.2 and uses it to curse; Prospero's verdict comes in 4.1; the masque of Ceres and Juno makes fertility itself a thing to be blessed and supervised.

techniques.name: Retrospective exposition
techniques.definition: Putting the backstory into a single long scene of telling rather than showing.
techniques.inThisBook: Act I Scene 2 is nearly a third of the play and consists largely of Prospero explaining the past to people who interrupt him. Because he controls what is told and when, the exposition is also a demonstration of his character.

techniques.name: The court masque
techniques.definition: A courtly entertainment of gods, song, dance and blessing, staged for an occasion rather than a plot.
techniques.inThisBook: The betrothal masque of 4.1 imports an entire Jacobean art form into the play and then breaks it off in the middle, which no masque at court would ever have done.

techniques.name: Metatheatre
techniques.definition: A play drawing attention to the fact that it is a play.
techniques.inThisBook: Prospero's actors are spirits, his revels end, the great globe dissolves, and the last speech asks the audience to release him with their hands. The illusion is dismantled in front of the people it was made for.

techniques.name: Song
techniques.definition: Sung lyric used to carry information a speech cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: Ariel's songs lead Ferdinand ashore, tell him his father is dead in language too beautiful to be grief, and wake Gonzalo in time to prevent a murder. The music does the work the plot would otherwise need scenes for.

techniques.name: Parody subplot
techniques.definition: A low plot that repeats the main plot's action in a debased form.
techniques.inThisBook: Stephano, Trinculo and Caliban plan exactly the crime Antonio and Sebastian plan, one scene apart, with a bottle in place of a sword — and are treated as a farce while the courtiers are treated as a threat.

techniques.name: The classical unities
techniques.definition: Keeping a play to one place, one day and one action.
techniques.inThisBook: Alone among the late plays, this one observes them: the characters repeatedly state the time, and the three hours of the story run at roughly the speed of the performance.

quotations.text: What cares these roarers for the name of king? To cabin: silence! trouble us not.
quotations.speaker: Boatswain
quotations.context: In the storm, ordering the king and his councillors below deck.
quotations.analysis: The play's first political statement is made by a working sailor to a monarch, and it is about the limits of titles. Within a hundred lines the audience learns that the storm was manufactured, so the one moment when rank genuinely counts for nothing turns out to have been arranged by a duke.

quotations.text: If by your art, my dearest father, you have Put the wild waters in this roar, allay them.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Her first words in the play, watching the wreck from the shore.
quotations.analysis: She knows at once that the storm is her father's doing, which tells the audience more about the household than any description could. The conditional 'if' is politeness rather than doubt, and the sentence ends in an imperative: the only person on the island who gives Prospero orders is fifteen.

quotations.text: What seest thou else In the dark backward and abysm of time?
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Testing how much Miranda remembers of her life before the island.
quotations.analysis: 'Backward' is used as a noun, which is not ordinary English then or now; the phrase makes the past a place you could fall into. He is checking the extent of her ignorance before deciding how much of it to repair, and the grandeur of the image conceals a piece of information management.

quotations.text: Hell is empty And all the devils are here.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Reporting how Ferdinand leapt from the burning ship.
quotations.analysis: Ariel is quoting a terrified boy, so the most famous line in the first act belongs to a character who never says it again. The joke underneath it is theological: the devils on this island are a spirit doing as it is told and a man who was once a duke.

quotations.text: Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains, Let me remember thee what thou hast promised, Which is not yet perform'd me.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: After performing the storm, before being sent out again.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is contractual rather than emotional: work has been done, a promise was made, the promise is outstanding. Prospero's answer is to recite the rescue from the cloven pine, which is the standard reply of an employer who would rather discuss gratitude than terms.

quotations.text: This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother, Which thou takest from me.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Answering Prospero's summons, before the quarrel about his attempt on Miranda.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the language of inheritance law — by his mother, therefore his — which is exactly how Prospero would argue for Milan. Nobody on stage disputes the facts; they change the subject to his conduct, and the play never returns to settle the question of title.

quotations.text: You taught me language; and my profit on't Is, I know how to curse. The red plague rid you For learning me your language!
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: The end of his argument with Prospero and Miranda about his education.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is delivered in fluent blank verse, which quietly contradicts it: he has plainly got more from the lessons than curses. 'Profit' is a merchant's word, and 'learning' here means teaching — the exchange is being audited, and the pupil finds it a bad bargain.

quotations.text: Full fathom five thy father lies; Of his bones are coral made; Those are pearls that were his eyes: Nothing of him that doth fade But doth suffer a sea-change Into something rich and strange.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Sung invisibly to Ferdinand, who believes his father has drowned.
quotations.analysis: The song tells a lie — Alonso is alive — in the gentlest possible form, turning a corpse into jewellery so that grief arrives already consoled. 'Sea-change' enters English here, and the whole lyric is an argument that loss can be transformation, which is the claim the last act will have to make good.
quotations.source: Globe/Moby text, 1.2.461-466; sung by Ariel within Ferdinand's scene

quotations.text: I' the commonwealth I would by contraries Execute all things; for no kind of traffic Would I admit; no name of magistrate;
quotations.speaker: Gonzalo
quotations.context: Imagining what he would do if he were king of the island.
quotations.analysis: The speech follows Florio's translation of Montaigne closely enough that the borrowing is visible, and Shakespeare stages it as a joke: Antonio and Sebastian point out that a commonwealth with no sovereignty has just been proposed by a man who began by saying he would be king of it. The mockery does not dispose of the idea, and the contradiction is the play's own.

quotations.text: And by that destiny to perform an act Whereof what's past is prologue, what to come In yours and my discharge.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Persuading Sebastian to murder the sleeping Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The line is now quoted as though it were wisdom about history; in the play it is a murderer's argument that the past is merely the warm-up and the killing is the real performance. 'Prologue' and 'act' are theatre words, put into the mouth of the man whose plot competes with Prospero's for control of the island's plot.

quotations.text: Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises, Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Reassuring Stephano and Trinculo, who have heard Ariel playing on an invisible pipe.
quotations.analysis: The drunkards are frightened and the so-called monster is the one who knows the island is safe. Shakespeare gives the play's most delicate verse to the character everyone on stage calls a beast, three minutes after he has explained how to drive a nail into a man's skull.

quotations.text: Remember First to possess his books; for without them He's but a sot, as I am, nor hath not One spirit to command
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Instructing Stephano on how the murder of Prospero must be done.
quotations.analysis: It is the most accurate piece of political analysis in the play, and it comes from the servant: the power is not in the man, it is in the library. Prospero lost Milan to his books and now holds the island by them, and the only character who understands the mechanism is the one with no share in it.

quotations.text: I am your wife, if you will marry me; If not, I'll die your maid: to be your fellow You may deny me; but I'll be your servant, Whether you will or no.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Proposing to Ferdinand at the log-pile, with Prospero watching unseen.
quotations.analysis: She proposes, sets out the alternatives and closes off the last of them: the grammar moves from a condition to a refusal to accept one. Having been given no information about her own life for twelve years, she takes the single decision available to her without consulting the man who arranged the meeting.

quotations.text: Our revels now are ended. These our actors, As I foretold you, were all spirits and Are melted into air, into thin air:
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Breaking off the wedding masque on remembering Caliban's conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: He is apologising to his son-in-law for a cancelled entertainment, and the apology grows into the play's largest statement about existence within eight lines. Note that he says 'as I foretold you': the consolation is that the disappearance was always in the design, which is true of a masque and is what he needs to believe about a dukedom.

quotations.text: We are such stuff As dreams are made on, and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The close of the same speech, before he admits his mind is troubled.
quotations.analysis: 'Made on' means made of, so human beings are built out of the same material as the vanished spirits — not that life resembles a dream but that it is cut from it. 'Rounded' can mean surrounded or finished off, and the line declines to choose, which is why it can be read as consolation or as the bleakest sentence in the play.

quotations.text: A devil, a born devil, on whose nature Nurture can never stick; on whom my pains, Humanely taken, all, all lost, quite lost;
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Alone, immediately after breaking off the masque.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is delivered by a man who has just spent years teaching the creature he says cannot be taught, and the repetitions — 'all, all lost, quite lost' — are those of someone arguing with himself. It is also the play's clearest statement of the position Miranda's existence contradicts.

quotations.text: Though with their high wrongs I am struck to the quick, Yet with my nobler reason 'gaitist my fury Do I take part: the rarer action is In virtue than in vengeance
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Immediately after Ariel says that he would pity the charmed courtiers if he were human.
quotations.analysis: The decision that ends twelve years of planning is made in four lines and prompted by a spirit. 'Rarer' means both more unusual and finer, which concedes that mercy is the less natural response; and the reason he gives is not that they deserve it but that it is the better piece of work.

quotations.text: But this rough magic I here abjure, and, when I have required Some heavenly music, which even now I do, To work mine end upon their senses that This airy charm is for, I'll break my staff, Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, And deeper than did ever plummet sound I'll drown my book.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Ending the long invocation of the elves of hills, brooks and groves.
quotations.analysis: He renounces the art in the middle of using it: the sentence that abjures magic also orders up the heavenly music that will disarm his enemies. The staff is broken, but the book is drowned deeper than any sounding line can reach, which is a peculiar precaution against an object he says he no longer wants.

quotations.text: How beauteous mankind is! O brave new world, That has such people in't!
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: On seeing the assembled courtiers for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The people she is admiring include the two men who set her adrift to die and a third who tried to murder his brother two days ago. Prospero's reply — three words, 'Tis new to thee — is the most economical piece of irony in Shakespeare, and it is the last thing he says to his daughter in the play.

quotations.text: Two of these fellows you Must know and own; this thing of darkness! Acknowledge mine.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Presenting the three conspirators to Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built to balance: two servants belong to the king, one belongs to me. 'Acknowledge' is doing a great deal of work — it can mean simply claiming a possession, or admitting a kinship, and the entire modern performance history of the play turns on which of those an actor decides to play.

quotations.text: As you from crimes would pardon'd be, Let your indulgence set me free.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The last two lines of the epilogue, spoken alone to the audience.
quotations.analysis: The man who has spent the play releasing or refusing to release other people ends by asking to be released himself, and the currency is applause. 'Indulgence' was also the word for a remission of punishment granted by the Church, so the audience is being asked to perform an absolution that the play's own theology could not quite supply.

timeline.label: Florio's translation of Montaigne published
timeline.detail: The English 'Of the Cannibals' behind Gonzalo's commonwealth speech becomes available.

timeline.label: The Sea Venture wrecked on Bermuda
timeline.detail: Bound for Virginia, the ship broke up on the reefs; the survivors reached Jamestown the following year.

timeline.label: Jourdain's A Discovery of the Barmudas printed
timeline.detail: One of the pamphlets that turned the wreck into a London story of storm, survival and abundant islands.

timeline.label: Performed before James I at Whitehall on 1 November
timeline.detail: The Revels record is the earliest firm evidence that the play existed and was being acted.

timeline.label: Played at court during the festivities for Princess Elizabeth's marriage
timeline.detail: One of a group of plays given by the King's Men that winter for the betrothal and wedding celebrations.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, and the volume opens with it — unusually well printed, with full stage directions and a cast list.

timeline.label: Dryden and Davenant's The Enchanted Island
timeline.detail: A Restoration rewriting that gave Miranda a sister and Caliban a mate, and held the stage for well over a century.

timeline.label: Peter Brook directs John Gielgud as Prospero
timeline.detail: At the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre; remembered for a Prospero of severity rather than serenity.

timeline.label: Jonathan Miller's colonial production
timeline.detail: Casting made the island's politics explicit, and helped establish a reading British theatre has not since put down.

timeline.label: Peter Greenaway's Prospero's Books
timeline.detail: A film that takes the library rather than the island as the centre of the play.

timeline.label: Julie Taymor's film, with Helen Mirren as Prospera
timeline.detail: Changing the magician's sex reorganises the play's questions about parenthood, exile and authority.

places.name: Milan
places.note: The dukedom Prospero lost to his brother while he studied.

places.name: Naples
places.note: Alonso's kingdom, and the wedding party the shipwrecked court was returning from.

places.name: Tunis
places.note: Where Claribel was married, and the voyage home from which the storm interrupts.

places.name: Algiers
places.note: Argier in the text: the city from which Sycorax was banished to the island.

places.name: Bermuda
places.note: The still-vex'd Bermoothes of Ariel's speech, and the site of the 1609 wreck behind the play's storm.

places.name: Whitehall Palace, London
places.note: Where the first recorded performance was given before James I on 1 November 1611.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest popular reading takes Prospero's renunciation of magic as the dramatist laying down his own art, and the epilogue as a retirement speech.
criticalViews.counter: It sits badly with the facts of the career: Shakespeare went on to collaborate on at least two more plays, and the epilogue is a conventional appeal for applause of a kind other plays also make.

criticalViews.position: The play as a colonial document
criticalViews.summary: Read beside the Bermuda pamphlets and the Virginia venture, the island becomes a place with an inhabitant, a claim and an occupation, and Caliban's case is the one the drama cannot dispose of.
criticalViews.counter: The Mediterranean geography is insistent — Milan, Naples, Tunis, Algiers — and a reading built entirely on the Atlantic has to work around it.

criticalViews.position: The play as a study of service
criticalViews.summary: A third approach puts Ariel rather than Caliban at the centre and reads the island as a workplace: promised wages, deferred release, labour that is invisible because it is magical.
criticalViews.counter: It risks flattening the difference between a spirit who is freed in the last scene and a man whose future the play never mentions.

essayQuestions.question: How far does The Tempest endorse Prospero's rule of the island?
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, service and the limits of art
plan: Begin with the fact that the audience is shown the storm before it is told who made it, so the first experience of his power is as a catastrophe.
Set Ariel's petition in 1.2 beside Caliban's claim in the same scene: two servants, two grievances, two completely different answers from the same master.
Use the breaking of the masque in 4.1 to show that his control is dependent on his attention, and collapses the moment he remembers a threat.
Weigh the decision in 5.1: mercy chosen freely, but only after a spirit has had to describe what pity is.
Close on the epilogue, where a man who has ruled everything asks an audience for the power to leave.

essayQuestions.question: 'The most eloquent character in the play is its slave.' Discuss Caliban.
plan: Establish what Caliban actually claims in 1.2 and note that nobody on stage denies the history, only changes the subject.
Examine the verse of 'the isle is full of noises' and ask why Shakespeare gives this speech to this character at this point in a conspiracy scene.
Balance the sympathy against 1.2 and the attempt on Miranda, which the play states plainly and does not excuse.
Compare his understanding of Prospero's power — take the books first — with the courtiers' failure to understand anything.
Finish with 'this thing of darkness', and with the play's silence about what becomes of him.

essayQuestions.question: What is the effect of staging the masque in Act IV and then interrupting it?
plan: Describe what a Jacobean masque was for: blessing, order, flattery of the ruler who paid for it.
Show how the Ceres and Juno masque fits that description exactly, down to the banishing of Venus and Cupid from the betrothal.
Identify the interruption as the only point where Prospero's plan is affected by something outside it.
Read the 'revels' speech as an attempt to convert a failure of stage management into a philosophy.
Consider the staging consequences: how a production makes the spirits vanish determines how seriously it takes the speech.

essayQuestions.question: Is the ending of The Tempest a reconciliation?
essayQuestions.focus: Forgiveness, silence and what is left unresolved
plan: List what is settled in 5.1: the dukedom restored, the marriage arranged, Ariel freed, the ship repaired.
Set against it what is not: Antonio says nothing, Sebastian jokes, Caliban's future is never mentioned.
Look closely at Miranda's 'brave new world' and Prospero's reply as a test of how much the audience is being asked to believe.
Use Gonzalo's summary at 5.1.235-241 — all of us found ourselves when no man was his own — and ask whether the play has earned it.
Decide what the epilogue changes: a character stepping out of the fiction to ask for pardon from people who have not been wronged.
